Minimal Filling Architectures of Polynomial Neural Networks: Counterexamples, Frontier Search, and Defects

Kevin Dao  and Jose Israel Rodriguez Note:  This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program under Grant No. 2137424. Any opinions, findings, and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation. Note: This research was partially supported by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation and by the National Science Foundation Grant No. 2510307.
Abstract

We provide a counterexample to the minimal unimodal conjecture for polynomial neural networks (PNNs) with power activation functions. Fixing the input and output widths, the conjecture states that any minimal filling architecture has unimodal widths for the hidden layers. We found a counterexample via a frontier search and certified it using recursive dimension bounds and symbolic computation. Notably, several subarchitectures of this example exhibit large defect, in contrast with the predominantly small-defect behavior observed in prior examples.

1 The Minimal Unimodal Conjecture

Neuroalgebraic geometry studies the geometry of function spaces parameterized by machine-learning models when they are algebraic or semi-algebraic in nature. It relates algebro-geometric invariants (e.g., dimension and singularities) to notions such as expressivity and training behavior [11]. This viewpoint involves other geometry-driven approaches in learning theory, including tropical-geometry descriptions of ReLU networks [14, 2]. In this article, we focus on polynomial neural networks; related neuroalgebraic analyses of model dimension and identifiability have also been carried out for other polynomial architectures, for example lightning self-attention [6].

We state the minimal unimodal conjecture in its original form, Conjecture 12 of [8], and recall the necessary definitions.

Definition 1.1.

A (feedforward) polynomial neural network (PNN) with activation function σ\sigma is a function of the form

pθ:ℝd0→ℝd0​p​t,pθ​(x)=W0​p​t​σ​W0​p​t−1​σ​…​σ​W1​xp_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}pt},\hskip 10.00002ptp_{\theta}(x)=W_{0}pt\sigma W_{0pt-1}\sigma\dots\sigma W_{1}x

where σ\sigma acts entrywise by (σ⁡(z))j=zjr(\sigma(z))_{j}=z_{j}^{r} for some r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}. The parameters are θ=(W1,…,W0​p​t)\theta=(W_{1},\dots,W_{0}pt), with each weight matrix Wi∈ℝdi×di−1W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{i}\times d_{i-1}}. The network’s architecture is the sequence 𝐝=(d0,…,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{0}pt), and the network’s depth is 0​p​t0pt.

It is immediate that pθp_{\theta} is a homogeneous polynomial map ℝd0→ℝd0​p​t\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}pt} and that pθ∈Symr0​p​t−1⁡(ℝd0)⊕d0​p​tp_{\theta}\in\operatorname{Sym}_{r^{0pt-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}})^{\oplus d_{0}pt}. Since homogeneous polynomials of degree D=r0​p​t−1D=r^{0pt-1} correspond to symmetric order-DD tensors, a depth-0​p​t0pt PNN induces a multi-stage factorization of such tensors.

Definition 1.2.

For fixed rr and architecture 𝐝\mathbf{d}, the map

Ψ𝐝,r:ℝd1×d0×⋯×ℝd0​p​t×d0​p​t−1→Symr0​p​t−1(ℝd0)⊕d0​p​t\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r}:\mathbb{R}^{{d_{1}\times d_{0}}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}^{{d_{0}pt}\times d_{0pt-1}}\to\operatorname{Sym}_{r^{0pt-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}})^{\oplus d_{0}pt}

given by θ↦[pθ​1…pθ​d0​p​t]T\theta\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}p_{\theta 1}&\dots&p_{\theta d_{0pt}}\end{bmatrix}^{T} where each pθ​ip_{\theta i} is a polynomial in the entries of the weight matrices is called the parameter map. The codomain is referred to as the ambient space, and its dimension is well known:

dim(Symr0​p​t−1⁡(ℝd0)⊕d0​p​t)=d0​p​t​(d0+r0​p​t−1−1r0​p​t−1).\dim\left({\operatorname{Sym}_{r^{0pt-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}})^{\oplus d_{0}pt}}\right)=d_{0}pt\binom{d_{0}+r^{0pt-1}-1}{r^{0pt-1}}.

The image of Ψ𝐝,r\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r} is a set of vectors of polynomials denoted ℱ𝐝,r\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{d},r} which we call the functional space. Its Zariski closure 𝒱𝐝,r=ℱ𝐝,r¯\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}=\overline{\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{d},r}} is called the neurovariety as it is an irreducible algebraic variety. To simplify notation, we remove rr from the subscript when the context is clear.

One goal of neuroalgebraic geometry is to characterize when the neurovariety and ambient space dimension agree.

Example 1.3.

Let 𝐝=(2,d1,1)\mathbf{d}=(2,d_{1},1), and denote the input variable into the network by x=[x1x2]T{x}=\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}&x_{2}\end{bmatrix}^{T}. If the weights are

W1=[11121d1],W2=[11…1],\displaystyle W_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 1&2\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ 1&d_{1}\end{bmatrix},\;\hskip 20.00003pt\;W_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&\dots&1\end{bmatrix},

then, Ψ(2,d1,1),r​(W1,W2)\Psi_{(2,d_{1},1),r}(W_{1},W_{2}) is the polynomial function

pW1,W2​(x)=(x1+x2)r+(x1+2​x2)r+⋯+(x1+d1​x2)rp_{W_{1},W_{2}}(x)=(x_{1}+x_{2})^{r}+(x_{1}+2x_{2})^{r}+\cdots+(x_{1}+d_{1}x_{2})^{r}

in Symr⁡(ℝ2){\operatorname{Sym}_{r}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}, i.e., an order-rr symmetric tensor in (ℝ2)⊗r(\mathbb{R}^{2})^{\otimes r}. ⋄\diamond

One reason for focus on the neurovariety is due to Proposition 5 of [8] which relates the dimension of a neurovariety 𝒱(d0,𝐚,d0​p​t),r\mathcal{V}_{(d_{0},\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt),r} with the expressivity of the functional space ℱ(d0,2​𝐚,d0​p​t),r\mathcal{F}_{(d_{0},2\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt),r}. By studying the neurovariety, one opens up the toolbox provided by algebraic geometry. A natural question is to study dimension (and other geometric properties) of the neurovariety. Dimension relates to the expressivity of the PNN. The study of the dimension of neurovarieties has been done in various works such as [8, 10, 4, 13, 12].

Definition 1.4.

The neurovariety 𝒱𝐝,r\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r} is said to be filling if 𝒱𝐝,r=Symr0​p​t−1⁡(ℝd0)⊕d0​p​t\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}=\operatorname{Sym}_{r^{0pt-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}})^{\oplus d_{0}pt}. If rr is fixed, we will say that the architecture 𝐝\mathbf{d} is filling if its neurovariety is filling.

We define a partial ordering on architectures of the same depth 0​p​t0pt by declaring that 𝐝′≤𝐝\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\leq\mathbf{d} if di′≤did_{i}^{\prime}\leq d_{i} for 0≤i≤0​p​t0\leq i\leq 0pt. If 𝐝′<𝐝\mathbf{d}^{\prime}<\mathbf{d}, we refer to 𝐝′\mathbf{d}^{\prime} as a subarchitecture of 𝐝\mathbf{d}.

Definition 1.5.

For fixed rr, an architecture 𝐝=(d0,…,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{0}pt) is minimal filling if 𝐝\mathbf{d} is filling and every subarchitecture 𝐝′=(d0,d1′,…,d0​p​t−1′,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}^{\prime}=(d_{0},d_{1}^{\prime},\dots,d_{0pt-1}^{\prime},d_{0}pt) with 𝐝′<𝐝\mathbf{d}^{\prime}<\mathbf{d} is not filling. We say it is a minimal filling architecture (MFA).

We are ready to state the minimal unimodal conjecture of [8].

Conjecture 1.6.

Fix r,0​p​t,d0,d0​p​tr,0pt,d_{0},d_{0}pt. If 𝐝=(d0,d1,…,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{0}pt) is an MFA, then there is an ii with 0≤i≤0​p​t0\leq i\leq 0pt such that

d0≤d1≤⋯≤di&di≥di+1≥⋯≥d0​p​t.d_{0}\leq d_{1}\leq\dots\leq d_{i}\hskip 20.00003pt\&\hskip 20.00003ptd_{i}\geq d_{i+1}\geq\dots\geq d_{0}pt.

That is, the sequence 𝐝\mathbf{d} is unimodal.

The motivation for the conjecture is that it conforms with “conventional wisdom”. In machine learning, the commonly held belief is that the network expands its capacity for feature representation to capture intricate patterns, and then narrows to refine these features for predictions. One reason to have believed this conjecture is that it holds in the shallow setting, where it follows from the Alexander–Hirschowitz theorem via the classical secant-Veronese dimension count.

2 The Counterexample: (2,3,4,5,4,6,4,1)(2,3,4,5,4,6,4,1)

Fix r=2r=2. Our main contribution addresses Conjecture 12 in [8].

Theorem 2.1.

The architecture 𝐝=(2,3,4,5,4,6,4,1)\mathbf{d}=(2,3,4,5,4,6,4,1) is a counterexample to the minimal unimodal conjecture. That is, it is minimal filling, and not unimodal.

The architecture 𝐝\mathbf{d} is clearly not unimodal. Our task is to show it is minimal filling.

Lemma 2.2.

For 𝐝\mathbf{d} as in Theorem 2.1, 𝒱𝐝,2=Sym26⁡(ℝ2)≅ℝ65\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},2}=\operatorname{Sym}_{2^{6}}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\cong\mathbb{R}^{65}.

Proof.

By Lemma 11 of [8], it would suffice to show that there is a θ{\theta} in the domain of the parameter map for which Jac⁡(Ψ𝐝,r​(θ))\operatorname{Jac}(\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r}({\theta})) has rank equal to 6565. Let rℝr_{\mathbb{R}} denote its generic rank. Since Ψ𝐝,r\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r} is given by polynomials with integer coefficients, one can consider instead the map over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and compute the generic rank rpr_{p} of that Jacobian. A finite field computation 11 1 All finite-field computations use the implementation of [10] to compute ranks of Jacobians over finite fields. finds a prime pp for which rp=65r_{p}=65. Since rp≤rℝ≤65r_{p}\leq r_{\mathbb{R}}\leq 65, it follows that rℝ=65r_{\mathbb{R}}=65. ∎

To show minimality, we utilize the following two lemmas.

Lemma 2.3.

[10] Let 𝐝=(d0,…,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{0}pt) and 𝐝′=(d0,…,di′,…,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}^{\prime}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{i}^{\prime},\dots,d_{0}pt) be two architectures except they differ in exactly the iith entry for 0<i<0​p​t0<i<0pt. Assume that di′≤did_{i}^{\prime}\leq d_{i}. Then,

𝒫𝐝′⊆𝒫𝐝&𝒱𝐝′⊆𝒱𝐝.\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{d}^{\prime}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{d}}\hskip 20.00003pt\&\hskip 20.00003pt\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}^{\prime}}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}}.

In particular, dim(𝒱𝐝′)≤dim(𝒱𝐝)\dim(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}^{\prime}})\leq\dim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}}\right). This does not depend on the choice of r≥1r\geq 1.

By induction, one can generalize Lemma 2.3 in the obvious manner: if 𝐝′≤𝐝\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\leq\mathbf{d} with d0′=d0d_{0}^{\prime}=d_{0} and d0​p​t′=d0​p​td_{0}pt^{\prime}=d_{0}pt, then dim(𝒱𝐝′)≤dim(𝒱𝐝)\dim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}^{\prime}}\right)\leq\dim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}}\right).

Lemma 2.4.

[8] Fix r≥1r\geq 1 and let k∈{1,…,0​p​t−1}k\in\{1,\dots,0pt-1\}. Then,

dim𝒱(d0,…,d0​p​t)≤dim𝒱(d0,…,dk)+dim𝒱(dk,…,d0​p​t)−dk.\dim\mathcal{V}_{(d_{0},\dots,d_{0}pt)}\leq\dim\mathcal{V}_{(d_{0},\dots,d_{k})}+\dim\mathcal{V}_{(d_{k},\dots,d_{0}pt)}-d_{k}.

By Lemma 2.3, 𝐝\mathbf{d} is minimal filling if the maximal subarchitectures obtained by decreasing a single hidden-layer width by one are not filling. These maximal subarchitectures are listed in table 1. The suggested dimension of these neurovarieties are obtained via finite field computations.

Proposition 2.5.

If the generic rank of rpr_{p} of the neuromanifold 𝒫𝐝,r\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{d},r} is equal to
dim(Symr0​p​t−1⁡(ℝd0)⊕d0​p​t)\dim\left(\operatorname{Sym}_{r^{0pt-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}})^{\oplus d_{0}pt}\right) for any prime pp, then 𝐝\mathbf{d} is a filling architecture. Moreover, the following architectures for r=2r=2 are filling:

(2,4,5,4)(2,4,5,4), (2,3,3)(2,3,3), (2,3,4,4)(2,3,4,4), (2,3,4,5,3)(2,3,4,5,3), (3,6,4,1)(3,6,4,1), (2,3,4,5,4)(2,3,4,5,4), and (4,6,3)(4,6,3).

The recursive bounds in Lemma 2.4 involve intermediate architectures whose filling status must be determined. Proposition 2.5 addresses the cases needed for the proof of the next lemma.

Lemma 2.6.

The ambient space is 6565 dimensional. The subarchitectures 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} for 1≤i≤61\leq i\leq 6 as described in Table 1 have dim(𝒱𝐝i,2)\dim(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d}_{i},2}) satisfying the bounds in the third column of the table.

3 Search Algorithm

Our algorithm for finding MFAs exploits Lemma 2.3 and the definition of minimality. The pseudocode is provided in Algorithm 1. To compute the dimension of the neurovariety, we use finite field computations. The difficulty in finding MFAs is due to the size of the search space.

To efficiently find MFAs (d0,𝐚,d0​p​t)(d_{0},\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt), we employ a frontier search over 𝐚=(d1,…,d0​p​t−1)∈[m,n]0​p​t−1\mathbf{a}=(d_{1},\dots,d_{0pt-1})\in[m,n]^{0pt-1}. We first prune the search space using naive dimension bounds, e.g., dim(𝒱𝐝,r)≤∑i=10​p​tdi​di−1−∑i=10​p​t−1di\dim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{0pt}d_{i}d_{i-1}-\sum_{i=1}^{0pt-1}d_{i}. If there were any previous searches already performed, then we prune the search space using the results. Then, we repeatedly test (d0,𝐚,d0​p​t)(d_{0},\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt) from among the remaining possibilities for filling architectures (d0,𝐚,d0​p​t)(d_{0},\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt):

  • •

    If (d0,𝐚,d0​p​t)(d_{0},\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt) is filling, we prune all 𝐚′>𝐚\mathbf{a}^{\prime}>\mathbf{a}.

  • •

    If (d0,𝐚,d0​p​t)(d_{0},\mathbf{a},d_{0}pt) is not filling, we prune all 𝐚′<𝐚\mathbf{a}^{\prime}<\mathbf{a}.

Eventually this terminates to a finite set of candidates. We verify each candidate by computing the dimension of its subarchitectures. If verification suggests a candidate is not minimal, then we adjust our mm and nn and run the search again. Utilizing previous search history to inform subsequent searches allowed us to quickly prune the search space.

4 Discussion

4.1 Minimal Filling Architectures

Fix d0=2d_{0}=2, d0​p​t=1d_{0}pt=1, and r=2r=2. Our search found 1313 MFAs of depth 0​p​t=70pt=7 with only one among them being nonunimodal: the architecture discussed in Section 2. For width 0​p​t=80pt=8, we found 8282 MFAs and among them, 2020 were nonunimodal 22 2 The repository includes the results of our search and the associated implementation. The list of counterexamples can be found in counterexamples.csv..

Fix d0,d0​p​t,r,d_{0},d_{0}pt,r, and 0​p​t0pt. By Dickson’s Lemma, one knows there are finitely many MFAs. The results of highly reliable finite field computations for p=231−1p=2^{31}-1 suggests that every entry in Table 2 is minimal filling. The proof is similar to the proof of Lemma 2.6, but with many more cases.

A natural next question is whether Table 2 provides an exhaustive list of MFAs for 0​p​t≤70pt\leq 7. For L≤7L\leq 7, we were able to verify that the entries are correct and the list is complete33 3 For details, refer to verify_exhaustive_list.md in the repository. At present, there is no comprehensive method for proving the completeness of such lists for large 0​p​t0pt. The main difficulty is that we do not know how wide we need to take the hidden layers to guarantee we found all minimal fillings.

4.2 Defectivity: losing expected expressive power

In studying the counterexample, we observed that its subarchitectures had large “defectivity”, a notion we recall next. Defectivity (for fixed activation degree rr) is a measure of an architecture’s loss in expressivity which cannot be attributed to expected symmetries. Presently, there does not appear to be a systematic understanding of which architectures are defective. This motivates the definition.

Definition 4.1.

If 𝐝=(d0,…,d0​p​t)\mathbf{d}=(d_{0},\dots,d_{0}pt), then the expected dimension of the neurovariety 𝒱𝐝,r\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}, denoted expdim⁡(𝒱𝐝,r)\expdim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}\right), equals the minimum of the dimension of the ambient space and ∑i=10​p​tdi​di−1−∑i=10​p​t−1di\sum_{i=1}^{0pt}d_{i}d_{i-1}-\sum_{i=1}^{0pt-1}d_{i}. The defect of the neurovariety is defined to be the difference expdim⁡(𝒱𝐝,r)−dim(𝒱𝐝,r)\expdim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}\right)-\dim\left(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{d},r}\right).

Example 4.2.

Using Algorithm 1, we found a counterexample to Conjecture 1.6 where d0=2d_{0}=2, d0​p​t=2d_{0pt}=2, r=2r=2, and 0​p​t=90pt=9 (See Figure Figure 2). The PNN with architecture 𝐝=(2,3,4,4,10,17,11,12,4,2)\mathbf{d}=(2,3,4,4,10,17,11,12,4,2) is minimal filling. This can be proved using the same techniques as in our first example. For i=1,…,0​p​t−1i=1,\dots,0pt-1, let 𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i} denote the architecture obtained by decreasing the iith hidden layer of 𝐝\mathbf{d} by one. Then

(codim⁡(𝒱𝐬i,r))i=10​p​t−1=(254,17,176,5,17,34,11,124).\left(\operatorname{codim}(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{s}_{i},r})\right)_{i=1}^{0pt-1}=(254,17,176,5,17,34,11,124).

Moreover, expdim⁡(𝒱𝐬i,r)=dim(Symr0​p​t−1⁡(ℝd0)⊕d0​p​t)\expdim(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{s}_{i},r})=\dim(\operatorname{Sym}_{r^{0pt-1}}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}})^{\oplus d_{0}pt}) holds for i∈{1,2,…,L−1}i\in\{1,2,\dots,L-1\}, hence defect⁡(𝒱𝐬i,r)=codim⁡(𝒱𝐬i,r)\operatorname{defect}(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{s}_{i},r})=\operatorname{codim}(\mathcal{V}_{\mathbf{s}_{i},r}). ⋄\diamond

The defects of some architectures in Table 1 turn out to be quite large. These appear to be among the first nontrivial examples of architectures exhibiting large defects. One can manufacture arbitrarily large defect by making one of the hidden layers have width one while allowing the remaining layers to be very wide. This motivates the study of maximal non-filling architectures and their defect.

It is well known that polynomial activations present a trade-off: low-degree polynomials can limit expressivity, whereas higher-degree polynomials often lead to numerical instability [15] and gradient explosion [5]. Efforts to address these issues are already present in the literature [7]. One natural response is to pair low-degree polynomial activations with architectures that are a priori highly expressive; in this context, understanding MFAs for power activations may inform architecture selection.

4.3 Next steps and new directions

Our results concern a classical feedforward PNN model with power activation. An important generalization is to allow broader polynomial activation families, for example activations expressed in orthogonal polynomial bases such as Chebyshev polynomials. A complementary direction is to investigate the polynomial networks (Π\Pi-nets) in [3] using tools from neuroalgebraic geometry, to obtain a geometric characterization of their expressivity.

Another next step is to compare training dynamics on MFAs versus maximal non-filling architectures. Several works have already investigated optimization landscapes and function-space geometry for convolutional neural networks [9] and PNNs [1] through a neuroalgebraic geometry lens. But a direct comparison between MFA and maximal non-filling architectures is yet to be studied.
